Title: Clarification on using third-party LLM APIs with the dataset                                                                                          
                                                                                                                                                                 
Hi organisers — thanks for putting this together                                                      
  
The Rules state that participants "will not release or otherwise grant data access to anyone" and must "establish appropriate safeguards to prevent  unauthorized data use". I'd like to check how this applies to LLM-assisted analysis, since part of the prize is Claude credits and I assume some API use is  anticipated.                                                                                                                                                   
                  
Four specific questions:

1. Does sending variant-level data from the VCF (e.g. coordinates, annotations, or rows of the file) to a hosted third-party LLM API count as "releasing or  granting data access"? Or is the restriction aimed at human recipients and republication?
2. If API use is permitted, does it depend on the provider's data handling — for example zero-retention or no-training-on-inputs terms? Would you want participants to document which provider and configuration they used?                                                                                           
3. How far does "derived datasets" extend for the deletion requirement? Are aggregate or de-identified artefacts — HPO term lists, candidate gene rankings, model prompts containing variant coordinates — in scope for the 30-day deletion, or only the source files?                                                     
4. Does the deletion obligation extend to data held in an API provider's logs, which participants cannot directly delete? If so, that would effectively require local or self-hosted inference, and it would be helpful to state that explicitly.                                                                      
                  
Happy for the answer to be posted publicly, as I suspect other participants will hit the same question.

Responses to Title: Clarification on using third-party LLM APIs with the dataset

Hello,
Thank you for your interest in the MVA Hackathon and for your important question. I am Sage's Chief Privacy and Compliance Officer. See my responses below, and please reach out if you need additional information. 

1. Does sending variant-level data from the VCF (e.g. coordinates, annotations, or rows of the file) to a hosted third-party LLM API count as "releasing or granting data access"? Or is the restriction aimed at human recipients and republication?

Answer: The restriction is intended to prevent granting control rights over the data, whether to a person or a service. The test we are applying is whether the service is a Processor or a Recipient. A service that processes data solely to return a result to you, takes no rights in it, and cannot use it for its own purposes is a tool, in the same way that Cloud storage, a hosted aligner, or a variant annotation API is a tool. A service that gains the right to use, retain, or learn from the data is a recipient, and sending it there is a release, whether the recipient is a person or a model. 
The rule is not about AI. Substitute any other piece of software you send data to, and the analysis is unchanged.  What matters are the terms attached to the service, and question 2 sets out what those terms have to say. 


2. If API use is permitted, does it depend on the provider's data handling — for example zero-retention or no-training-on-inputs terms? Would you want participants to document which provider and configuration they used?

Answer: Yes, it depends on the terms. Two conditions must hold:
-- No Training on your inputs or outputs, and no rights taken by the provider in either. If the provider can learn from the data or use it for its own purposes, it is a recipient, not a tool.
-- Retention is limited in time and purpose. Zero retention is not required. Short-lived logs kept for abuse monitoring, debugging, or service quality are acceptable, provided the provider cannot use the content for any other purpose.
Two cautions: 
a) Turning training off is not always complete: some providers still use the content you give feedback on, or content flagged for safety review. Make sure you opt out and do not rate outputs. 
b) Credit or grant programs sometimes attach their own terms that override your account's defaults, so read the terms attached to any credits you are using rather than assuming your account settings govern.
Please record the provider, the plan or tier, and the relevant setting in your methods description. A line is enough, for example, "Anthropic API, Claude Sonnet, Commercial terms, no training on customer content"


3. How far does "derived datasets" extend for the deletion requirement? Are aggregate or de-identified artefacts — HPO term lists, candidate gene rankings, model prompts containing variant coordinates — in scope for the 30-day deletion, or only the source files?

Answer: Only the material that carries the child's genome. Your findings are meant to survive and, in fact, are meant to be published: submissions are CC BY, and the results remain available to the research community.
DELETE: 
-- The VCF, BAM and CRAM files, and any copy, subset, slice, or reformat of them, including index files.
-- Intermediate files that carry per-variant genotypes, at genotype scale such as filtered or annotated variant tables, along with caches and notebook state holding them.
-- Stored prompts or logs on your own systems that contain pasted blocks of variant data.
-- Any model weights, embeddings, or fine-tunes trained directly on the raw genomic data.
KEEP:
-- Your ranked candidate variant list, which is your submission.
-- The human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) terms.
-- Gene and pathway rankings, mechanism analyses, drug candidates.
-- Your code, report, pitch, and leaderboard entry, all devoid of any prohibited data or material in the delete list above. 
The rule of thumb for anything in between: a handful of named variants in a report is a finding. A genome-wide table of the child's genotypes is the dataset in a different file format. If an artifact would let someone reconstruct a meaningful portion of the genome, delete it. 


4. Does the deletion obligation extend to data held in an API provider's logs, which participants cannot directly delete? If so, that would effectively require local or self-hosted inference, and it would be helpful to state that explicitly.

Answer: No, and local inference is not required.
The deletion obligation applies to what you control: your machines, cloud instances, notebooks, repositories, storage, etc. It does not extend to short-lived logs held by a service provider that you cannot reach. The same is true of any cloud service you would use in this work.
What bounds that residual retention is the condition in question 2. If your provider cannot train on your content and cannot use it for its own purposes, and if its logs are time-limited and kept for abuse monitoring or service quality, that sits inside what these rules contemplate. If a provider's terms allow it to keep or learn from your content indefinitely, the problem is not the log; it is that you should not have sent the data there.

When you confirm deletion at the 30-day mark, attest for the systems you control and note the provider and configuration you used.

Dear Sage MVA Hackathon team,

Thank you for the detailed clarification above. I have one follow-up regarding a specific setup.

I am participating as an independent/citizen-science participant and use ChatGPT Plus as a coding and research assistant. OpenAI states that when “Improve the model for everyone” is disabled, new conversations are not used to train its models. Temporary Chat is also not used for training and is deleted after 30 days, with limited retention/review for abuse monitoring.

Would ChatGPT Plus used with model training disabled — preferably in Temporary Chat — satisfy the Processor criteria described above for handling patient-specific findings or derived information? Or should controlled/patient-specific information only be sent to services operating under business/API terms?

Until this is clarified, I will keep the controlled genomic data and patient-specific derived information out of ChatGPT and use it only for code development, methodology, public-source research and non-sensitive project work.

Thank you very much for clarifying this.

Best regards,

ChartyBaby

latest.raw:
Hi ChartyBaby,

Thank you for the careful approach in the meantime — genuinely appreciated, and exactly the right instinct while this gets clarified.

To apply the Processor vs. Recipient test from above: the distinction that matters isn't really "ChatGPT" vs. "Claude," it's which terms actually govern the specific product tier you're using. Consumer subscription products (like ChatGPT Plus) are typically governed by general Consumer Terms of Service, which historically reserve broader usage rights to the provider than a Business/API tier agreement does — even with training toggled off. Business and API tiers, by contrast, usually come with terms specifically structured around no-training and limited-purpose retention, which is closer to what @cfsuver's Processor test is actually looking for.

So our current guidance would be: for anything involving patient-specific or controlled genomic information, use the Business/API tier of whichever provider you choose, not the consumer subscription product — even with training disabled and Temporary Chat enabled. Consumer-tier toggles reduce risk, but they don't necessarily meet the "no rights taken, time-limited retention only" bar the same way Business/API terms are designed to.

In the meantime, ChartyBaby — your current approach (keeping controlled/patient-specific data out of ChatGPT entirely, using it only for code/methodology/public-source research) is a safe default and exactly in line with the "conservative interpretation" guidance Luca gave earlier in this thread.

Hi all, here is an update confirmed guidance on consumer-tier LLM use

Thank you all for your patience while we got this properly confirmed with our governance team.

To correct my earlier reply: consumer-tier accounts (e.g., Claude Free/Pro, ChatGPT Plus) are permitted for use with patient-specific or derived information, not just Business/API tiers — provided both of the following hold:

1. You opt out of model training through your account settings.
2. You do not provide feedback on outputs (thumbs up/down, ratings, etc.), and your content is not flagged for safety review — both platforms' terms note that opted-out content can still be used for training in these two specific cases, so avoid them if you're working with sensitive derived information.

As before, please document the provider, product tier, and training-opt-out setting you used in your methods description — a line like "Claude Pro, training opt-out enabled, no feedback provided" is enough.

Apologies again for the earlier overcorrection and thank you all for bearing with us as we worked through this properly.
